claim: Problem finders (art students who explored and rearranged objects longer before drawing) made work that independent experts rated as more original; the study followed careers.
title: The Creative Vision: A Longitudinal Study of Problem Finding in Art
n: art school students (exact n not verified)
transfer: Add a problem-finding step before solving: spend a fixed budget exploring and reformulating the task, then choose the framing. Use only on open tasks.

claim: Intelligence was not correlated with studio performance or later professional success in the Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi art cohort (as reported by a review).
authors: Review of Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi (1976) in Project MUSE
title: Review of The Creative Vision
transfer: Raw ability is a trait; the behaviour (exploring the problem) is what to copy.

claim: Familiar solutions block better ones in expert chess players: experts said they searched for a better move but their eyes kept returning to features of the first move (Einstellung).
quote: expert chess players reported that they were looking for a better one. But their eye movements showed that they continued to look at features of the problem related to the solution they had already thought of.
title: Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung (set) effect
transfer: Self-reported search for alternatives is not evidence of it. Force a rival generation step that does not see the first answer, then compare. Supports our divergence gain but warns that same-context doubt stays anchored.

claim: In an eye-tracking replication, experts who chose the familiar suboptimal move kept looking at it; experts who found the best move gradually disengaged attention from the familiar move.
quote: were able to gradually disengage their attention from the Einstellung move
title: The Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions of the Einstellung Effect in Chess: Evidence from Eye Movements
transfer: Disengagement is a behaviour: drop the first solution from view (fresh context) before searching again.

claim: Einstellung has a boundary: when the familiar move was a blunder, all experts and most novices avoided it. When it was good but suboptimal, 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose it.
quote: when the Einstellung move was a blunder, all of the experts and the majority of the novices were able to avoid selecting the Einstellung move
title: The Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions of the Einstellung Effect in Chess: Evidence from Eye Movements
transfer: Fixation costs most when the first answer is good but not best. A cheap check of whether the first answer is clearly wrong or merely adequate could route to rival search. Matches our finding that doubt hurts when the first answer is right.

claim: Luchins water-jar studies: after several problems solved by a long method, people kept using it on a problem with a simple solution; a control group without the priming found the simple one at once. Telling people not to be blind helped more than half.
title: Mechanization in problem solving: the effect of Einstellung
transfer: Few-shot examples of one method can lock the model into it. Test with and without worked examples; add a prompt to re-check for a simpler route. Source opened is a secondary page.

claim: Deliberate practice explained 26% of performance variance in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and under 1% in professions.
quote: deliberate practice is important, but not as important as has been argued
title: Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
transfer: Practice amount is a training-time trait, not a runtime step. Lesson: structured domains (games) gain more than open ones. Figures come from a search summary, not the paper itself.

claim: A music-only meta-analysis with a broader practice definition found a larger effect, so the deliberate practice effect size depends on how practice is defined.
title: The influence of deliberate practice on musical achievement: a meta-analysis
n: 13 studies; rc = 0.61 (reported in the Hambrick et al. commentary I fetched)
transfer: none (training-time finding). Be careful quoting one 'practice explains X%' figure.

claim: Hambrick and colleagues state deliberate practice accounted for about one third of the reliable variance in each domain, leaving most variance to other factors.
quote: accounted for about one-third of the reliable variance in performance in each domain
authors: Hambrick, Oswald, Altmann, Meinz, Gobet, Campitelli
title: Facing facts about deliberate practice
transfer: none (trait and training level). Do not build a schema on 'practice makes expert'.

claim: A double-blind replication of the classic violin study did not reproduce the core finding that practice amount matched each skill level; the effect was real but smaller (eta squared 0.26 vs 0.48 original).
quote: We did not replicate the core finding that accumulated amounts of deliberate practice corresponded to each skill level.
title: The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Romer (1993)
transfer: none at runtime. Marks the classic claim as overstated; teacher-designed practice added no variance over practice alone.

claim: Original claim: individual differences in ultimate performance are largely explained by amounts of past and current practice.
quote: individual differences in ultimate performance can largely be accounted for by differential amounts of past and current levels of practice
title: The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
transfer: none (quote taken from the replication paper, not the original). Superseded in strength by a-07 and a-10.

claim: Masters recalled real chess positions after brief viewing far better than novices but were no better on random positions (all about 3 to 4 pieces), pointing to chunks rather than larger memory.
quote: all players, from master to novice, recalled only about three or four pieces on the average on random positions
title: Perception in chess
transfer: Expertise is stored patterns. For an agent: retrieve stored solved cases and patterns for the problem type instead of reasoning from scratch (lessons ledger).

claim: Template theory extends chunking: players also use long-term memory templates; masters are estimated to store about 50,000 chunks; experts beat novices on random positions given enough time.
title: Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
transfer: Store lessons as templates with variable slots, not as free text.

claim: Experts sort physics problems by deep principle; novices sort by surface features (objects, wording).
quote: Experts tended to categorize by the major physics principles used in the solution to the problem.
title: Categorization and representation of physics problems by experts and novices
transfer: Probe step: ask the model to name the underlying principle or problem type before solving, and route on that, not on surface wording. Veldhuis found advanced novices show both.

claim: Incubation (a break from a problem) has a small positive effect on problem solving; divergent thinking tasks benefit more than insight tasks; longer preparation helps; a demanding break task reduces the effect.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
n: 117 studies; mean d about 0.29 to 0.32, divergent tasks d about 0.65 (figures disagree across secondary sources, not confirmed in the paper)
transfer: Partly transferable: a model has no unconscious work. The analogue is a fresh-context restart after a first attempt. Do not claim the human mechanism.

claim: Intelligence and creativity correlate weakly (about r = .17, about 3% shared variance) in a meta-analysis of about 21 studies.
title: Meta-analysis of the relationship between creativity and intelligence
n: 21 studies, 45,880 participants (secondary report; a 2021 meta-analysis of 112 studies found r = .25)
transfer: none: a trait result. Suggests a stronger base model alone will not give more novelty, so schema steps matter.

claim: Feist's first meta-analysis of personality and creative achievement found creative scientists and artists more open and less conventional; scientists more conscientious than non-scientists; the largest effects were medium.
title: A meta-analysis of personality in scientific and artistic creativity
transfer: none: personality traits cannot transfer. A persona prompt is possible but unproven.

claim: Weisberg argues genius creativity rests on ordinary thinking; case studies (Darwin notebooks, Watson on DNA, Picasso sketches, Edison) show no special divergent thinking process.
title: Creativity: Beyond the Myth of Genius
transfer: Build novelty from small steps: reuse and modify prior knowledge, and check each step. Argues against a pure random divergence step. Evidence is case-study, not controlled.
